status: pilot census of explicit historical shipment/container identifiers surviving on modern bound objects
central_claim: Historical shipment/container identifiers survive across support types, languages and documentary states. They are relational keys, not markers of a single material or linguistic class. Exact numeric addresses must be separated from identifier-present-but-unread cases.

evidence_classes.EXACT_TWO_LEVEL_NUMERIC_ADDRESS: box/item or equivalent multi-level old address explicitly transcribed by the catalogue
evidence_classes.EXACT_NUMERIC: single historical sack/box number explicitly transcribed
evidence_classes.IDENTIFIER_PRESENT_VALUE_UNREAD: catalogue states that an old identifier survives but does not reproduce its value

cross_class_findings: Shipment/container identifiers occur on Nepali hand-made paper, imported paper and machine-made paper.
They occur on local-language source texts, English derivative/copy states and bilingual/multilingual metadata surfaces.
The same identifier system can therefore link documents across material and linguistic classes.
Historical container identity must be coded separately from support, language and modern shelfmark.
vol.6 provides an exact two-level historical address, Box 2 / Item 12, attached to a modern volume composed overwhelmingly of machine-paper English copies.
Numeric address nodes and unread-identifier nodes must not be treated as equivalent evidence in the reconstruction graph.
source_control_rules: Do not reconstruct unread identifier values omitted by the online catalogue.
Do not equate box/sack numbers across dates without content-level confirmation.
A cover number proves historical container assignment, not direct textual descent.
Identifier language does not determine the language or origin of the underlying document.
Old addresses may have been renumbered at repacking events; repeated numerals across inventory states are candidates, not identities.
